name: Rosa Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start with an eight o'clock lecture on data structures, which I attend even though it's recorded, because I focus better in the room. After lunch there's a lab or a maths tutorial, and three evenings a week I play volleyball for the university's second team. I share a flat with two girls from home, and on Sundays we all cook one big pot of something and argue about whose turn it is to buy washing-up liquid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in software engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was good at maths and my dad is an accountant, so I grew up thinking about numbers as a job. But I wanted to build things, not just count them. My mum teaches primary school and my dad has a small accountancy office with three staff. They pay my fees and rent, I have no debt, and I use an AI assistant now and then for explanations when the lecture slides don't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd shrug. I'd say the tools are handy for a few things, like summarising notes or reformatting a table, and then nothing much beyond that. My friends would argue, but I'd say let's see how things look in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a little uneasy, but about my dad's office, not about me. Even a quiet AI world means cheap software for invoices and tax forms, and his clients ask why they should pay him if an app does it. He has already lost two small clients to online tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and join a student project team to get real experience. I'd keep using the assistant now and then. I'd also offer to help my dad set up better ways to handle small jobs, maybe with templates, so he spends less time on routine forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay with a small knot in the stomach, mostly when my dad talks about next year's rent for the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of that worry is about your dad's office specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it. My mum's job as a teacher is safe, but my dad's income is the bigger part of the household. If the office shrinks, we'd feel it, even if my fees are already paid for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Dad, you're the one who explains things to clients in plain words, and an app can't do that yet. I'd suggest he focus on advice instead of forms. I'm not sure he'd listen, since he's proud of how neat his forms are.

say: I'd shrug and say the tools are **handy** for summaries and tables, nothing more.
I'd say to friends: let's see in a few **years**.
think: I'm a little **uneasy**, not about me but about my dad's office.
He has already lost two small **clients** to online tools.
do: Join a student project **team** for real experience.
Keep using the assistant **now and then**.
Help my dad set up **templates** for routine forms.
feel: Okay, with a small **knot** in the stomach about the office rent.
S0.quote: I'd say to Dad, you're the one who explains things to clients in plain words, and an app can't do that yet.
fieldNote: Calm about herself, but **already** carries a household worry: her father's accountancy income.
Practical and measured; offers help in small, concrete ways.
Her mother's teaching job is treated as the safe anchor in the family.

steps.text: Join a student project team building a real app
Set up form templates to save her dad time
Use the AI assistant for tricky lecture explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a manageable one, if people get time and help. I'd tell my dad's clients to use the tools wisely, and I'd tell my friends to get used to checking AI output, because that will be a job in itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be properly worried now. Checking, planning and writing numbers are exactly what the card says go first, and that's my dad's whole business. His office might lose half its work in a few years. My degree is more exposed than I'd like, since entry-level coding is what software takes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my degree and aim for areas where software meets the real world, like medical devices or embedded systems. I'd take a placement year if my university offers one. I'd also help my dad try one of the AI bookkeeping tools so he's the one offering it to clients, not losing clients to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow squeeze. Not a crisis, but I can feel the walls moving a bit closer each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How realistic is it that your dad would adopt these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd resist at first, because he's careful about client data. But he's not stubborn about things that save time. If I show him one that keeps the data on his own computer, I think he'd try it. I'd set it up on a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen in your household if his office did shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would cut holidays, and my mum might take on private tutoring. They'd keep paying my rent because they've promised, but I'd feel guilty and take a part-time job to ease it. I'd rather take a part-time job than watch my parents worry.

say: I'd say it's a big change but **manageable** with time and help.
I'd tell friends that checking AI output will be a **job** itself.
think: I'm properly **worried**, since checking and numbers are my dad's whole business.
My own entry-level **coding** field is more exposed than I'd like.
do: Aim for **embedded** systems or medical devices, where software meets the real world.

feel: A slow **squeeze**: I feel the walls move closer each year.
S1.quote: I'd rather take a part-time job than watch my parents worry.
fieldNote: The household's main **income** is exposed, and she says so; that drives the mood.
Plans to bring the tools to her father rather than wait for them to hit him.
Would take a part-time job despite family money, from guilt and loyalty.

steps.text: Pick embedded systems and medical device modules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on, this can't be dealt with by shrugging. Two years is far too short for firms and families, so we'd need governments to protect people's income while this settles. I'd tell my friends to ask their parents what savings they have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be really scared. My dad's office would be gone within about a year or two, because clients would use software. Mum's school job stays, but that's one income for a family of four. I'd be thinking about my own degree and whether anyone will hire a second-year student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same week about money: what to cut, what to keep, and whether they should sell the office early at a fair price. I'd stay at university, since leaving would not help, and I'd try for hands-on work like electronics or lab assistant jobs. I'd cut my own spending hard and offer to move to a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being told a bridge you rely on has a crack, and you can't tell how long it will hold. I'd lose sleep on this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your parents how bad you think it is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, because my dad respects numbers. I'd say: here's what happens if your income drops by half, here's our spending, here's what we cut. I'd show it on a spreadsheet and not cry about it, at least not in front of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops you from simply hoping it's slower than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the sort who'd rather prepare for the bad case than be caught out. If it's slower, I've lost nothing but a few weeks of comfort. That's a trade I'd take every time.

say: I'd say shrugging isn't enough and we need **income protection** from governments.
I'd tell friends to ask their parents what **savings** they have.
think: I'd be really **scared**, because my dad's office could be gone within two years.

fieldNote: Expects the household's **main earner** to lose his income, which moves her to alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to help people if we start right away. I'd say my dad's profession needs a plan, like moving from forms to advice, and I'd say governments should fund retraining for people his age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. I'd graduate in three years right into the thick of it, but I'd have time to build skills and a CV. My dad's office would shrink but he'd have a few years to change what he sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and look for a placement and a first job in something close to hardware. I'd help my dad learn the AI tools and talk to a business adviser about moving his office to advice for small shops. I'd save my part-time earnings and keep my spending modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long runway, but a short one, depending on the day. I'd go between feeling busy and feeling anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change what you'd do with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd be thinking about selling the office. In five, we could change what the office does, like helping small businesses with plans and cash flow, which software can't do as well. It's about using the time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Persuading him. He's spent thirty years being the person who gets the forms right. Switching to a role where you're a coach and not an expert is hard. But I'd rather argue with my dad now than after the clients have gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent amount of time, so the sensible thing is to prepare calmly. I'd say schools and universities should change what they teach, and workers my dad's age should be offered training at a pace that's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, if a bit watchful. I'd graduate, work a few years, and be in a good position by 2036. My dad would be near retirement, so his office might simply close naturally, which is a different thing from being forced out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree, join a placement year, and look for a first job somewhere stable. I'd keep using AI tools at the level I do now, and add more when they're normal. I'd help my parents plan their pension, because that's where I could actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty calm. I'd still look around at the news and notice when things move faster than expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for as a sign that ten years was too optimistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If big companies stopped hiring new graduates in a whole field for a year, or if the school my mum teaches in started using AI tutors for core lessons. Those would be real signs to me, much more than predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell younger students anything different in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say study what interests you and learn two or three things well, a technical skill and a people skill. And don't spend your first year terrified, because I wasted a few weeks doing that in the other pictures.

say: I'd say ten years is decent, so prepare **calmly**.
I'd say workers my dad's age should get training at a **fair** pace.
think: I'd be fine but **watchful**, in a good position by 2036.
My dad's office might close **naturally** near his retirement.
do: Finish the degree, take a **placement** year and find a stable first job.
Add AI tools **gradually** once they're normal.
feel: Pretty **calm**, while watching for things that move faster than expected.
S4.quote: Study what interests you and learn two or three things well, a technical skill and a people skill.
fieldNote: The decade lets the household **absorb** the change; her father's office could close at retirement.
Names clear warning signs: graduate hiring freezes and AI tutors in her mother's school.
Mood stays uneasy because the family income question lingers, not because of her own prospects.

steps.text: Finish the degree with a placement year at a hardware firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my dad's office would be gone before anyone could plan. What would help is income support for self-employed people and training that pays while you study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to ask the quiet ones what they think. I don't shout online, but I'd be the person doing the budget while everyone else argues.

headlineQuote: I'd be the person doing the budget while everyone else argues.
portrait: Rosa is an 18-year-old **software engineering** student, the daughter of an accountant and a primary school teacher.
She is pragmatic and centrist, uses an AI assistant now and then, and prepares for the bad case.
Her fear is about her **father's office**, the household's larger income, more than her own job.
She plans with spreadsheets and quiet persuasion, and offers to take a part-time job.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year picture and eases as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because her father's office would be gone before anyone could plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for self-employed people and training that pays while you study.
